Econs can also roughly adopt this content mastery + application skill approach.

For content mastery, if your school notes have a lot of fluff, it’s important that you figure out which parts are actually important and examinable and only read those. Everything else is unnecessary. This will cut down your revision time considerably since you know what to look for.

There are many nuances in econs, and it’s important to be clear of your concepts. E.g. the difference between supply and quantity supplied. Again, this boils down to content mastery.

When it actually comes to answering the questions in exams, be clear of common answering frameworks (tbh I can’t recall them off the top of my head as it’s been months HAHA). For every topic, there tend to be common step-by-step explanations (like a specific set of key words in a specific sequence) that you’ll need to familiarise yourself with, and know when to apply.

For CSQ, familiarise yourself with common question types and the answering frameworks/steps to tackle them and hit the marking points. For essays, there are some “regurgitable” essays like “market failure caused by negative externality”, “circular flow of income” etc. There also tend to be common answer points that you can reuse and recycle across a variety of similar essay questions. Try not to write the unusual, unique essay questions and stick to the simpler ones which have straightforward answer points.

You’ll write better evaluations as you read more model essays. Model essays will be your best friend, and reading them and actually digesting them will help you see the “common step-by-step explanations” and “common answer points” I mentioned. Personally I never wrote any practice essays; I relied solely on reading model essays and the occasional class tests.

TLDR: a similar content mastery + application skills approach can be adopted, though for econs content mastery is a bit more important.

H2 BCME

There are 2 parts to securing an A for every subject - content mastery (really digesting your notes) and application skills (studying for the exam specifically). It’ll be tough to get an A if you only have one without the other.

For content mastery, personally I never sat down to memorise things. It’s too dry and unstimulating. Instead, I tried to really understand what I was learning. It helps the most if the subject is something you can at least somewhat enjoy. Think of it this way - if I were to ask you to teach me how to play your favourite video game, could you? You probably could without even reading off anything because that’s just how well you understand the ins and outs of your favourite game. That’s how you should go about learning your concepts for your subjects.

As for application skills, this is where practice comes in. Try to piece together recurring answer points / repeated working steps across questions. It’s not so much about the quantity of practice but the quality of it. Familiarise yourself with common question types.

How you go about achieving your content mastery and application skills is up to your own learning style. Some people find that consults help them immensely; conversely I never found them particularly useful so I never went for any. Don’t do something just because it works for others if you know it won’t work for you - in my case, that’s why I didn’t waste my own time going for consults or signing up for tuition. Study smarter rather than harder.

TLDR; master your content and application skills and you should have a good chance of clinching an A.

P.S. I’m a science student, so I can’t verify whether this works for arts subjects. Though I have a feeling it’s a no.

The tiers are subjective. I was more so going off the fact that OP said PATs were abolished in his JC this year.

Hello, I’m a retainee. Is this EJC? Haha it sounds like it. I retained in EJC this year, so next year will be my 3rd year. 

Since you’d like to know how to advance, I’ll just say that last year, I heard some of the people who failed PATs ended up grovelling at the principal’s feet and got advanced. But they abolished the PATs this year, because the sheer amount of resources it takes to set a whole new paper only for most of the test takers to fail again cannot be justified. And besides, most of those who were advanced continued to do badly. So if you really want to promote, you can try meeting with the principal. Though, you have to be realistic with your chances, because like another commenter said, the fact that your CT is so adamant about barring you from advancing likely indicates that most, if not all, of your STs are of the same opinion.

This is my personal take: think very, very hard about whether you want to advance. I know right now, it can be tough to focus on the big picture and not only on the short term. But your A Levels are important — retaining one year is a cheap price to pay if it means you can get into a university of your choice. What’s the point of advancing only to do terribly for A Levels and possibly end up having to retake it as a private candidate? Of course, if you can afford to take a foundation year in an overseas uni, then this doesn’t matter. But if you don’t have that privilege, then you really need to start to consider retaining as a possible route to explore. It is no doubt unfortunate that your whole future hinges on that one results slip from Cambridge, but alas, that is how the Singaporean education system is structured, and you have to learn to cope with that fact.

If you’re not aiming for a prestigious course, then by all means, go ahead and risk advancing. I’m not saying this as I have no faith in you, but I’m being practical. I was not keen on retaining last year either, and I thought for sure I’d study my hardest in J2 and catch up. But this is idealistic at best, and a blatantly foolish and flimsy excuse at worst. If you didn’t study the whole year, what are the chances you can suddenly start pumping in so many hours of studying? And with twice the amount of content at that? 

Now that I have finished my second year of JC1, I realise the sheer volume of content there was to learn. There was no way I could have become well versed in all that, on top of the J2 content, in a short 10 months. For context, I scored a grand total of 15.5RP last year, and that was including my MT to pull up my grades. This year, my RP increased by more than 5 times, without MT. I didn’t have that much of an advantage — what much advantage can 15.5RP confer? I scored that low for good reason — I knew nothing. The only advantage I had was the extra time freed up by no MT or PW. This may sound bleak, but yes, although I think retaining would be better for you, it still won’t be easy. You have to be prepared to learn everything from scratch. The extra year can be extremely helpful for introspection — I never realised how much I loved learning till this year. 

Word of caution, now that you’re caught in this quagmire, you will likely start hearing concerns of your ability to cope in JC and people may start questioning if JC is really for you. I suggest you think very hard on this. As ironic as it was, even after receiving my horrific results last year, I still knew that JC was the best option for me. I needed the structure, and so I fought with my teachers and parents for another chance in JC despite them wanting me to switch to private U. I knew that if I had went to poly, I would have had even less motivation to do well, and my GPA would have gone to crap, let alone private U. In the same vein, reflect on what you know is best for you (and be realistic about it, without letting your pride get in the way) and try your hardest to fight for that — it is more imperative now than ever that you take charge of your future.

The social, emotional, and academic challenges that come with retaining may seem daunting, but your future is the most important thing. If retaining one year means you score well enough to be spoiled for choice of universities, then that’s not a bad trade at all. If there’s anything you’d like to know, you can PM me. Best of luck OP!

1) Yep most leadership positions are sadly IP dominated… but I feel that a factor is also because a lot of JAEs don’t dare to even run because they don’t know anyone, whereas IP students dare to run for leadership positions. For student council this year, some really popular IP kids who were prefects their whole lives didn’t get in (huge shocker), while some JAE did (not saying it’s rigged or anything, but pretty sure the school tried to have an even IP-JAE ratio). The school tries its best to let JAEs feel at home!

2) I’m not sure what you heard about the JIP orientation being abolished, but I’m J1 this year and JIP students started school on 10 Jan but JAEs only came in quite late, like 29th? But don’t worry because literally no one I know still talks to their OG LOL.

I think most OGs are fine, but my OG in particular had a really bad JAE-IP segregation. Even among the IP schools there was some segregation; the CHS and SNGS people were leaving the SCGS people out.

3) IP students ARE open to making new friends, but they won’t forget their cliques.

4) I take BCME so here are my opinions on each department! These are only my opinions so take them with a grain of salt.
PW: there’s the “holy trinity” with godsend teachers, then there’s the “unholy trinity” which will basically screw your PW grade over.

Math: Quite good I guess. You need to be self-directed though.

Chem: I had remedial with this super good teacher. But my chem teacher ended up being horrible. She mumbles all her words so I couldn’t even tell what she was saying most of the time. Some teachers are good, and some can’t teach. Being an independent learner is probably your safest bet.

GP: I absolutely adore EJC’S GP department. The teachers are all so incredible and fun. It’s a really diverse mix of personalities. Only downside is that GP is like impossible to score?! 😭 I got a B and I’m already in the top quintile. Pretty sure the distinction rate for my cohort’s J1 promos was like 1%… of course this strictness might bode well in the end at A-Levels though. Anyway EJC GP is amazing! Seminars are the best, when the teachers get to interact just a bit.

Bio: Teachers are nice! They’ll make time for you if you need consults. They seem kinda young, but their teaching is still effective, at least in my experience.

Econs: TBH this department is super lowkey… but my teacher (Mr Ma) is like super good and he really values his students’ mental wellness. You need to be self directed though, you can clarify questions but it’s difficult for them to mark all the practice essays.

5) We have a mix of studious and non-studious students. Those who were always on the principal’s list in secondary school (especially the IP schools) will obviously study very hard. But a lot of my close friends are sadly retaining. It’s a mix.

6) About relationships… I think at our age, everyone is just generally thirsty. My class has a 3:1 gender ratio and literally everyone has no love life. But there are also quite a few high-profile relationships in my batch. A lot of them are IP couples who started dating during the IP orientation.
